name: Canaanite City-States and Emerging Israelite Highlands
note: Approximate cultural zones, not a single political border: surviving Canaanite city-states occupied much of the plains and valleys, while early Israelite settlement is most strongly associated with the central hill country. The outline follows the western highlands and Galilee and deliberately excludes most of the Philistine coastal plain and deep Negev.

name: Traditional United Monarchy of Israel
note: Conservative approximation of the core territory traditionally associated with Saul, David, and Solomon. Scholarly reconstructions differ substantially, so this polygon shows the central settled core rather than the Bible's widest tributary claims.

references.title: Bible Odyssey — History and the Bible

name: Kingdom of Israel
note: Approximate Iron Age northern kingdom centered first at Shechem and Tirzah and later Samaria. The outline follows Galilee, the Jezreel Valley, Samarian highlands, and parts of the Jordan Valley; control of peripheral areas changed repeatedly.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Kingdom of Judah
note: Approximate hill-country kingdom centered on Jerusalem, extending through the Shephelah when political conditions allowed and south toward Beersheba. Its western and southern limits varied, especially under Philistine, Egyptian, Assyrian, and Babylonian pressure.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Moab
note: Approximate Iron Age Moabite kingdom east of the Dead Sea. Its durable core lay between the Arnon/Wadi Mujib and the Zered/Wadi al-Hasa, while Mesha's ninth-century claims extended north onto the Madaba plateau. Earlier biblical references are not mapped here as proof of an established territorial state.

references.title: ASOR/BASOR — Mesha’s Moab and the Madaba Plateau

name: Ammon
note: Approximate Iron Age Ammonite highland kingdom centered on Rabbath-Ammon. The core occupied the upper Jabbok/Zarqa plateau; eastern steppe influence and western limits varied and cannot be drawn as a fixed frontier.

references.title: ASOR — Iron Age kingdoms of Jordan

name: Sihon's Amorite Kingdom (Biblical Reconstruction)
note: A literary-geographical reconstruction of Sihon's kingdom between the Arnon and Jabbok, centered on Heshbon. It is not an archaeologically recoverable fixed frontier and should be read as the region described by the biblical narrative.

references.title: Bible Odyssey — History and the Bible

name: Og's Bashan (Biblical Reconstruction)
note: A literary-geographical reconstruction of Bashan north of the Yarmuk, encompassing the Golan and Hauran toward Ashtaroth and Edrei. The polygon is an approximate landscape zone, not a demonstrable state boundary.

references.title: Bible Odyssey — History and the Bible

name: Edom
note: Approximate late Iron Age kingdom in the southern Jordanian highlands between the Dead and Red Seas. Assyrian texts securely attest named Edomite kings in the eighth and seventh centuries BCE; debate continues over whether an earlier mobile polity should also be called Edom.

references.title: ASOR — The Emergence of Edom: Recent Debate
ASOR — Southern Jordan and the Negev

name: Philistine City-State Zone
note: Approximate southern coastal plain organized around Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron after Egyptian withdrawal around 1150 BCE. Philistia was a changing network of city-states, not a state with a single permanent border; Babylonian campaigns ended its independent political life around 604 BCE.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Philistines and Sea Peoples
Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Aram-Damascus
note: Approximate kingdom centered on the Damascus oasis, extending through the Anti-Lebanon approaches and, at periods of strength, toward the Golan and Hauran. This is narrower than the former generic Syrian rectangle.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Phoenician City-State Coast
note: Narrow coastal and island zone of the Phoenician city-states, principally Tyre, Sidon, Byblos, and Arwad. The Lebanon ranges sharply constrained the inland extent, while political unity and exact boundaries varied by city and period.

name: Amalekite Association Zone (Biblical Tradition)
note: A deliberately broad literary association zone for episodes set in the Negev and adjoining deserts. No independently established Amalekite territorial state or archaeologically recoverable frontier is known; the dates follow the narrative setting rather than an archaeological polity.

references.title: Bible Odyssey — History and the Bible

name: Midianite Association Zone
note: Approximate northwestern Arabian zone east and southeast of the Gulf of Aqaba, with connections across caravan routes into the southern Transjordan and Sinai. Midianite mobility makes any hard frontier misleading.

name: Neo-Assyrian Expansion in the Levant
replaces: Assyrian Imperial Sphere in the Levant
note: Approximate and changing Neo-Assyrian military and tributary sphere from the western campaigns of Shalmaneser III to the fall of Samaria. This was not uniform direct administration: local kingdoms including Israel, Judah, Damascus, and the Philistine cities alternated among resistance, tribute, vassalage, and annexation.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Neo-Assyrian Provinces and Vassals in the Southern Levant
replaces: Assyrian Imperial Sphere in the Levant
note: Approximate southern-Levantine zone after Assyria annexed the northern kingdom. Former Israelite territory and parts of the coast were provincially administered, while Judah and several neighboring kingdoms generally remained tribute-paying vassals. Control contracted during the empire's late seventh-century collapse.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Neo-Babylonian Rule in the Levant
note: Approximate Levantine territories brought under Neo-Babylonian rule after the defeat of Egypt and Assyria. Judah was conquered and Jerusalem destroyed in 586 BCE; other western polities were subdued at different moments. The polygon shows the western imperial zone, not a single unchanged provincial border.

name: Yehud Medinata under Achaemenid Rule
replaces: Persian Yehud and the Achaemenid Levant
note: Approximate small Persian-period province of Yehud centered on Jerusalem within the larger satrapy of Across-the-River. Its exact limits changed and remain debated; this replaces the former polygon that incorrectly represented most of the Levant as Yehud.

name: Ptolemaic Judea
replaces: Hellenistic Judea and the Eastern Mediterranean
note: Approximate Judean district during sustained Ptolemaic control after the Wars of the Successors. Administrative boundaries are incompletely known and the wider region remained contested; the map therefore shows Judea rather than an undifferentiated eastern-Mediterranean empire.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Seleucid Judea before the Maccabean Revolt
replaces: Hellenistic Judea and the Eastern Mediterranean
note: Approximate Judean district after Seleucid conquest of Coele-Syria and before the Maccabean revolt. This is a local administrative approximation, not the boundary of the full Seleucid Empire.

references.title: Metropolitan Museum — Eastern Mediterranean and Syria

name: Warsaw Ghetto
note: Approximate outline of the German-established Warsaw ghetto. The ghetto was ordered in October 1940, sealed in November, repeatedly reduced after mass deportations in 1942, and destroyed following the 1943 uprising; no single polygon is valid for its entire existence.
